name: Fatima Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Fatima, 43, with a music bachelor’s. I play cello in the theatre pit, the musicians’ area below the stage, record short rehearsal parts for two choirs, and teach six older pupils after school. I am an experienced working player, about average in a good section. I like the moment everyone breathes together before the first note; I hate having a recording used again without another fee.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that work sit with life at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner repairs lifts on a regular contract, and we have two children in school and a mortgage. My music income is high for this work, and we have about nine months of expenses saved. There are many other music posts nearby, although a posted vacancy is still different from a job offer. I have never used an AI tool; I prefer my pencil marks on the score.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the pit players that a tidier booking email is useful if the theatre still pays people for rehearsals. I expect the six pupils and choir recordings to carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage is manageable with nine months saved and my partner’s steady contract. I still check the recording licences, because an ordinary reuse dispute can cost a fee without any new AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d play the scheduled pit shows and keep six pupils this term. This week I’d ask both choirs to confirm paid recording dates and reuse terms in writing, then put a cleared recording fee into the mortgage reserve each month if those dates hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our income in this mild picture. An untidy contract irritates me, but one delayed fee would not change the children’s dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make an ordinary recording fee disappear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A choir might use the same practice part for a second season without asking. I would point to the signed terms before making another part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the new software for booking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used an AI tool. I would let the office tidy its calendar, but I would still check my paid dates on paper.

say: I would accept a cleaner **booking calendar** if rehearsal fees remain clear.
I would ask choirs to put **reuse terms** in writing.
think: Our **nine-month reserve** and two incomes make a routine delay manageable.
A reused **practice part** can still lose me an ordinary fee.
do: Keep **pit shows** and six pupils this term.
Confirm **recording dates** and reuse terms, saving a cleared monthly fee when dates hold.
feel: I feel **calm** because current paid work and savings cover a routine delay.
S0.quote: An untidy contract irritates me, but one delayed fee would not change the children’s dinner.
fieldNote: Her **strong reserve** and partner’s regular wage support calm under a mild technology change.
She checks **recording rights** on paper and has never used AI.

steps.text: Keep scheduled pit shows and six pupils this term
Save one cleared recording fee monthly if choir dates hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the union that cheap generated practice parts could cut a real line in a musician’s invoice. I would ask for a minimum recording fee and written permission before old parts are reused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The choir parts make about a fifth of my music pay, so losing them would reduce what we save. I can still teach and play the pit, but a high salary on paper does not make one lost stream harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d bring my choir invoices to the musicians’ union and ask for a shared reuse clause. In the first year, if part orders fall, I’d stop hiring the outside recording room on empty days and keep the paid pit and pupils while asking the theatre for written dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about a lasting cut to my own fees, though we can cover a transition. I dislike being told a recording is free because a machine can copy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your work changes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first lost order would be a cello guide for a choir learning its harmonies. A generated cello practice recording can arrive before a robot joins our theatre band.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn an AI recording tool yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would rather negotiate the fee for playing than buy a new subscription. If the theatre later requires one, I would first ask what data it takes from my pupils.

say: I would ask the **union** for recording fees and consent before reuse.
I would explain that **generated guides** can undercut paid cello parts.
think: Choir recordings supply **one fifth** of my music income.
Live **pit shows and pupils** remain paid, but a lasting cut shrinks savings.
do: Bring **choir invoices** to the union this month for a shared reuse clause.
Stop **room hire** on empty days if orders fall; keep paid pit shows and pupils.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a sustained cut to my own recording pay.
S1.quote: A generated cello practice recording can arrive before a robot joins our theatre band.
fieldNote: Her threatened **recording fees** are a measurable fifth of income despite strong savings.
She seeks **collective terms** and cuts unused room hire if orders decline.

steps.text: Ask musicians’ union for minimum fees and recording reuse consent this month
Stop outside recording-room hire on empty days if choir orders fall
Keep paid pit shows and six pupils while bookings continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the pit that thinking AGI in 2028 could make choir guides and schedules cheaply, while capable playing robots follow around 2031. I would not count those three years as a contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the choir recording fees to end quickly, and the theatre may also shorten the pit season. Nine months saved gives us time to look, but I cannot replace a fifth of my pay by hoping another choir calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I’d get the pit’s paid season dates and ask the union for written reuse terms. In the first year after 2028, if recording orders stop, I’d end outside room hire at renewal and apply for an advertised music-school cello post only if the school accepts my degree and experience and its written net wage covers travel and school pickup; I’d keep the pit and six pupils until a written offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about losing a regular slice of income, not overwhelmed. Our nine-month savings are a bridge, not a replacement wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge a school offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the teaching hours, net wage and pickup time in writing before giving notice at the theatre. A job title without paid hours would be a poor trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the children during an audition?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner could collect them on his early shift, if that week’s rota allows it. I would confirm that before travelling to the school.

say: I would distinguish **2028 thinking AGI** from robot players around 2031.
I would ask the union for **written reuse terms** before recording orders end.
think: I expect **recording fees** to end and pit dates could shrink.
Our **nine-month savings** buy search time, not replacement income.
do: Keep pit shows and **six pupils** until a written job offer; confirm paid dates before 2028.
End **room hire** at renewal if 2028 recording orders stop.
Seek an **advertised school post** after 2028 only if orders stop, credentials accepted and written net wage covers travel and pickup.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing a regular fifth of my pay.
S2.quote: Our nine-month savings are a bridge, not a replacement wage.
fieldNote: Thinking AGI threatens **choir guides** before robots can play cello around 2031.
A school move needs **accepted credentials**, a written net wage and a workable pickup schedule.

steps.text: Keep paid pit shows and six pupils until written school offer
End outside recording-room hire if 2028 orders stop at renewal
Seek advertised school post if 2028 orders stop, credentials accepted, written net wage covers travel/pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a 2031 arrival gives us a few years to put a paid teaching group on its feet. Thinking AGI would reach the choir parts before robot cellists around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could replace some recording fees with an adult chamber group, but only if people actually pay for my preparation. I will not use the mortgage reserve to test an empty room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I’d ask the independent library for a room without a deposit and invite eight adults to prepay for a six-week chamber group. I’d start only if those fees cover my teaching and preparation time and my partner’s rota covers pickup; in the first year after 2031 I’d repeat it only if eight still pay enough for my time, the room stays free and pickup remains covered, while keeping paid pit dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about recording fees shrinking over the next few years. That time would let me test one class without betting the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first expense you would refuse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would refuse a room deposit. If the library cannot offer the room free, I would keep the pupils I already teach and look for another space.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would prepare music for the group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would choose simple parts and do the preparation myself. Eight prepaid places must pay for preparation hours too, or the circle is unpaid work.

say: I would explain that **2031 thinking AGI** precedes robot cellists around 2034.
I would offer a **paid chamber group** only with real registrations.
think: A chamber group could replace **choir fees** if eight adults pay.
I will not spend the **mortgage reserve** on an empty room.
do: Ask the library for a **free room** next spring; start only if eight prepay teaching and preparation and pickup is covered.
Repeat the **group** after 2031 only with eight payments covering teaching and preparation, free room and covered pickup; keep paid pit dates.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my own recording fees shrinking, with time to test one group.
S3.quote: Eight prepaid places must pay for preparation hours too, or the circle is unpaid work.
fieldNote: Her **group price** includes preparation hours, not just the six sessions.
The **free room** and pickup plan keep the family reserve out of the experiment.

steps.text: Start six-week library group with free room, eight prepayments covering teaching/preparation and pickup arranged
Repeat group after 2031 if eight cover teaching/preparation, room free and pickup covered
Keep paid theatre pit dates while bookings continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my children that a decade is enough time to learn how a fair fee is written down. Thinking AGI comes around 2036, and robot cellists follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I may still have the pit chair, but a ten-year warning does not guarantee its next contract. Our savings and my partner’s work make the coming few years secure enough to plan without panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d keep six pupils and pit dates and transfer a cleared recording fee into our mortgage reserve when one arrives. Through the decade I’d run the adult group only if the library room stays free, eight people prepay enough for teaching and preparation, and pickup is covered; in the first year after 2036 I’d keep it only while those payments cover my work and seek an advertised school post if pit dates end, with accepted credentials and a written net wage that covers travel and pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distant contract, not frightened of this month’s mortgage. A ten-year warning helps me insist on a price for my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy equipment now to prepare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would repair my present cello before buying anything new. The recording fee goes to our reserve only after it clears, not when a client promises it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave the pit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would leave only for a real school offer with written hours and pay. A rehearsal calendar can still be worth more than a vague teaching title.

say: I would keep **2036 thinking AGI** separate from robot cellists around 2039.
I would teach my children to ask for **written fair fees**.
think: At **53**, I may still hold the pit chair without a guaranteed next contract.
Our **strong reserve** and partner’s work allow careful planning now.
do: Keep **pit and pupils** until a written school offer; save a cleared recording fee when received.
Run the **adult group** only with free room, eight prepayments covering preparation and teaching, and covered pickup.
Keep the **paid group** after 2036; seek advertised school work if pit dates end, credentials accepted and written net wage covers travel/pickup.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about distant contracts while current bills remain manageable.
S4.quote: A ten-year warning helps me insist on a price for my work.
fieldNote: Her **current cushion** permits deliberate savings and a no-deposit teaching trial.
A post-2036 **school move** requires pit loss, credential acceptance and a written viable wage.

steps.text: Keep paid pit dates and six pupils until written school offer
Save one cleared recording fee into mortgage reserve when paid

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because it could end the choir parts before a school job opens. Written pit dates, union recording terms and an advertised school position with accepted credentials and enough net pay for pickup would help. I could use our savings to search, but I would not call a vacancy an offer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the hours spent preparing a lesson or a rehearsal part. A musician can fill every day and still be giving some of the work away for free.

headlineQuote: A musician can fill every day and still be giving some of the work away for free.
portrait: Fatima is a **43-year-old cellist** with a music bachelor’s, pit work, choir recordings and six pupils.
Her **higher pay**, regular partner income, mortgage and nine-month reserve support two school-age children.
She **never uses AI** and seeks written recording terms through the union.
Fast AGI threatens **choir fees** before robot players; she tests prepaid chamber teaching and considers a real school vacancy.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** could end choir-guide income before an acceptable school job opens.
whatWouldHelp: Written **pit dates** and union recording terms would protect pay during the search.
An advertised **school post** accepting her credentials and covering travel and pickup would offer replacement wages.
